speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: VIET NAM-POSSIBLE COMPOSITION OF SUGGESTED CONTROL BODY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to get some explanation from the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Last night he appeared on the television news and, among other things, said he hoped one of the countries participating in the international police action in Viet Nam could be communist China. I should like to ask him whether he has any information on the attitude of communist China. What has been the reception in the United States, officially, in this connection? In view of the fact that he mentioned in his remarks that he would expect Canada would participate, has he any more information than he had yesterday in that regard, as to what might be expected to be Canada's contribution?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VIET NAM-POSSIBLE COMPOSITION OF SUGGESTED CONTROL BODY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian participation would, of course, be related to whether it were a United Nations obligation. Yesterday we anticipated limitations on that possibility but Canada, as a member of the United Nations, might be a country whose services would be enlisted. As to whether Canada would accept, one would have to examine the circumstances at the time. The suggestion made by the Prime Minister is one which would have to be filled in as a result of the negotiation that would take place if and when a cease fire in Viet Nam was arranged.
With regard to the participation of communist China, the suggestion had been that the presence to be set up might be composed of the Geneva accord powers, and that would include China. The reply I made was predicated on that assumption. This too is a circumstance that would depend upon negotiations following a cease fire. There was no need to communicate either of these particular propositions to any particular government.

However, I might say that the general suggestion made by the Prime Minister in New York on Friday is being viewed with interest, and in some quarters I may say with more than interest. These are considerations that have to be studied carefully, and they are being studied by the countries with which we have already been in contact.

subtopic: VIET NAM-POSSIBLE COMPOSITION OF SUGGESTED CONTROL BODY
speechtext: Would the minister say which of the countries have shown a great deal of interest in this proposal; because press references indicate the United States is not interested in it. What are the countries the minister has in mind which he describes as displaying that avid interest?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VIET NAM-POSSIBLE COMPOSITION OF SUGGESTED CONTROL BODY
speechtext: I am sure my hon. friend would agree that the suggestion is one that does warrant avid interest. But he, perhaps better almost than anyone else in this house sitting on that side, would agree that it would not be desirable, when measures of this sort are being discussed, to disclose more than is necessary.

subtopic: VIET NAM-POSSIBLE COMPOSITION OF SUGGESTED CONTROL BODY
speechtext: May I compliment the minister by saying that the latter part of his answer represents the general tenor of all his answers. May I ask him this. Were any of these countries communicated with before the Prime Minister made that speech to the Canadian club in New York?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VIET NAM-POSSIBLE COMPOSITION OF SUGGESTED CONTROL BODY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, these matters have been discussed in a general way with a number of interested countries; not only the particular suggestion but the general problem.

speechtext:

subtopic: VIET NAM-POSSIBLE COMPOSITION OF SUGGESTED CONTROL BODY

subtopic: VIET NAM-POSSIBLE COMPOSITION OF SUGGESTED CONTROL BODY

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the governments even more directly concerned than we are- considerably more directly concerned-have already been discussing among themselves, through diplomatic channels, the possibility of negotiation in this matter, and we have been participating in those diplomatic discussions.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Industry. Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Transport. I know the minister is aware that an ice jam at the mouth af the Thames river has caused a sudden flood that has covered thousands of acres of Kent county farmland with water and has forced the evacuation of citizens from some of the local communities. Inquiries of the Ministry

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: THAMES RIVER, ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR FEDERAL ASSISTANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have taken immediate steps by way of aid in this very serious situation. The hon. gentleman spoke to me about nine o'clock last night, and I think before ten o'clock some action had already been taken on the matter, and further action has been taken today. I spoke this morning to my colleague the Minister of National Defence, and a helicopter is being provided with a view to expediting in every way we can the breaking of the ice at the mouth of the Thames river before a lot of valuable agricultural land in Ontario is flooded.

speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, March 8, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-136, to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors-Miss LaMarsh-Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Order. House again in committee of the whole on Bill No. C-136. When the committee rose yesterday clause 8 of the bill was being considered.
On clause 8-Amount of employee's contribution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I mentioned yesterday that under clause 8 it is proposed

to deduct from the Canadian worker's pay cheque a further amount over and above what is already being deducted. As I said, deductions are made in respect of federal income tax, provincial income tax, union dues and, in many cases, for health insurance. And now, on top of all that, a further deduction will be made for the pension plan.
I wonder where the line is to be drawn concerning compulsory deductions from the Canadian worker's pay cheque? It seems to me there are already too many deductions. His earnings are taken away from the Canadian citizen and no matter how hard he works, new laws are passed authorizing further deductions from the Canadian worker's pay cheque, as we will be doing under Bill No. C-136.
Personally, I have nothing against giving the old age pension to Canadian citizens at 65 years of age, but I would much prefer that the same amount be given to everybody, whether or not the citizen had a high or low income. But I do object to further deductions from pay cheques, as proposed under clause 8.
Rather I think the government should consider increasing old age pensions regularly, without any contributions on the part of the workers. A stop should be put to those deductions from pay cheques for all kinds of plans such as the one we are considering today.
It is my opinion that when a Canadian citizen has been working all week, he surely deserves his salary and he should keep it because he really needs it to pay rent, food, clothes, schools, medicine, doctor, etc.
Here is another plan which will deprive the Canadian worker of another part of his salary.
I protest against the fact that once again, the government assumes the right to take away, through this pension plan, other parts of the Canadian worker's salary.
I am in favour of an increase of the old age pension to $100, that is under part IV of the pension plan, that such a pension be given, without a means test, to all Canadian citizens aged 65. But I am against the deduction of any amount from the worker's pay, as it is proposed to be done under clause 8.
I am the more opposed to such a proposal that the 1.8 per cent deduction will constitute a much larger amount than what the worker will get back as a pension.
The 1.8 per cent which will be collected from both the employer and the employee will not be used only to pay a pension to
Canada Pension Plan
Canadian citizens at the age of 65; the combined contribution of 3.6 per cent-1.8 per cent for the employer and 1.8 per cent for the employee-will be used to build up a bigger fund than needed to pay pensions to Canadians, and I do not find that normal. Not only will money be taken away from Canadian citizens for the pension plan, but that money will also be used to set up a fund the government will use for other purposes.
When money is thus taken from Canadian citizens and employers, it is no longer a pension plan, but an additional tax imposed on Canadian taxpayers, a further burden on the low income groups.
I most strongly object to this, and I am against this further tax levied on Canadian taxpayers. Since the coming into power of this government, taxes have constantly been increasing and, under clause 8 of Bill No. C-136, an additional tax is being imposed on the Canadian taxpayers.
I hope that the Minister of National Revenue will put an end to all those taxes. I see him sitting next to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is absent at the moment and the Minister of National Revenue, that is the minister of taxes, is piloting the bill. Why? Because he is looking after the interests of his department and not only those of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The big advantage of this pension plan is that the minister of taxation will go and pick even more money out of the taxpayers' pockets by increasing taxes. That is why he comes here to defend this pension plan.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Order. It would seem to me that the hon. member is overstepping the limits of clause 8 now before us. He appears ready to undertake a general study of the taxation problem in Canada.
On reading clause 8, I see that it deals with the employee's contribution under this bill. I would suggest that the hon. member, having made his point, can conclude his remarks when he wants, but he should refer to the subject matter now before us, that is the amount of employee's contribution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
I was speaking precisely on clause 8, which reads as follows:
Commencing with the year 1966, every employee who is employed by an employer in pensionable employment during a year shall, by deduction as provided in this act-

Canada Pension Plan
That is a mandatory deduction. How do you call that? It is a tax. Therefore, under clause 8, a new tax is levied to set up this pension plan.
I maintain that my remarks are in order when I state that the 1.8 per cent contribution collected from the employee and the 1.8 per cent contribution paid by the employer, a total of 3.6 per cent, represent more than the amount needed to pay a pension to people of 65 as contemplated by the minister. Therefore, when more money is collected than is paid out, there is more money than is needed to set up a pension fund, since there is some left over. In that respect, it is estimated that between $8 and $9 billion will be collected within 10 years. That is not a pension fund; it is a new tax.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Would the hon. member allow me a question?
Can the hon. member tell us why his colleagues and himself talked so much yesterday
in order to have several groups of people included in the pension plan, knowing that it was a contributory plan, and today they are against imposing any form of contribution?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will tell my hon. friend from Longueuil (Mr. Cote) that I am not against the paying of a pension to all citizens. But I object to the fact that they must pay three times the amount which they will draw at the age of 65. I object to this, and I will never be a party to the legalized robbery which is being organized by the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of National Revenue.
I am not against Canadian citizens receiving $100, $125 or $150, not when they have reached the age of 70, but at 65; to the contrary, I am in favour of such a measure, because I realize that they deserve it, but I object to the fact that at the age of 18, 20, 30, 40 and 50 a Canadian citizen should pay three times the amount he will receive when he is 65. He must pay four times the amount he will receive, and he is compelled to pay that amount. That is why I claim that this is another tax, and when this is done under a pension plan, this is an act of hypocrisy and legalized robbery committed by the Minister of National Revenue. If the hon. member for Longueuil accepts that he is very na'ive and he does not defend the interests of the people of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I ask another question?

Does the hon. member know that in 20 years the reserve fund of the pension plan accumulated out of the contributions will have been exhausted as a consequence of the benefits paid to the contributors to the Canada pension plan?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Longueuil may believe the beautiful speeches delivered by the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of National Health and Welfare, but we do not, because if the fund is exhausted 20 years hence, that will be due to the fact that the other departments which are always broke will have dug into that fund in order to pay anything but pensions.
If it is emptied, it will also be due to the poor administration of both departments concerned, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of National Revenue, since expenditures of $18 million are expected when there is not even a single pension to pay to anybody. When expenditures of $18 million are expected for the administration of a pension plan under which no pensions are paid, I appreciate that this can keep two ministers busy to mismanage the business of the Canadian people.
Therefore I would ask the hon. member for Longueuil not to blame us, but rather the two ministers.
I can understand that two ministers are needed to try and make us swallow that, because the Canadian people will not digest it, for they are not as credulous as the hon. member for Longueuil.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
I prefer to believe the estimates of actuaries rather than those of the hon. member for Lapointe.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: There is no point of order.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I merely
answered the question of the hon. member for Longueuil and I must remind him that our role is not to take everything at its face value, to accept everything without asking questions. If it were so, I would tell him to go back home. Besides, it is a fact that for a long time he has merely been acting as a rubber stamp.
I was saying that under this pension plan, the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of National Health and Welfare take away from Canadian citizens, in a compulsory way, more money-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Order. It seems that the hon. member is considering now the very principle of the bill. This principle has already been discussed in the house, considered in committee and passed; unanimously or not, it was passed by the committee and by the house, and I do not think that the hon. member can now raise the question of the principle of the bill.

Therefore I invite him to restrict his remarks to that clause.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I call your attention to the fact that I am not discussing the principle of the bill, but rather the 1.8 per cent paid by the employer and by the employee, that is 3.6 per cent, and I submit that those contributions make up an amount too large in relation to the pension benefits offered. The contribution is provided for in clause 8, and I think I am in order when I say that the percentage is too large in relation to the benefits that the pensioners will get.
I am speaking strictly to the provisions of clause 8, that is the percentage of the salary that will be taken out of the pockets of the Canadian taxpayer, and when I compare that amount, under the provisions of clause 8, I say it is too large for the pension plan alone, and that is why I should like to suggest to the Minister of National Revenue to lower that contribution or to increase the benefits of the pension plan.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think that my remarks are relevant because I am sticking to the provisions of clause 8. In fact, I am discussing the contributions that will be compulsory for the employers and the employees. So, I believe I am completely in order.
In fact, some of my colleagues, in a few minutes, will bring forward figures to establish that it is highway robbery to levy 3.6 per cent from the taxpayers for the purposes of this pension plan, and that is precisely what I am objecting to. That is the reason why I say that the amounts to be levied for the purposes of this pension plan, under clause 8 of Bill No. C-136, are too high, and I have no hesitation in describing this pension plan as a colossal hypocrisy that is offered to the Canadian people under the cover of social security legislation.
As a matter of fact, the Canadian taxpayer will be further taxed, and that is why Lib-
Canada Pension Plan
eral members of parliament are so strongly upholding the pension plan.
Mr. Chairman, I want to voice my objection to all these taxes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext: This is not a tax.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hear some hon. members say that this is not a tax, but when a plan is compulsory, as specified in clause 8, and when deductions are made from the salary, as provided under clause 8, when a taxpayer is liable to be fined and even jailed if he does not pay, as provided under clause 8, then I call that a farce. And when people are taxed under false pretences, as specified under clause 8, then I call that hypocrisy and legalized theft, and the members of the cabinet and of this government are responsible.
Mr. Chairman, they do not know what means to take to impose further taxes; therefore they go about it indirectly under the provisions of clause 8.

The people of Queens-Lunenburg riding whom I represent are a very independent group of people. They are a highly industrious and thrifty group of people. Many of them realize that it is their thrift and industry which, in part, helps keep the government in spending money, and not the other way around. Many of these people are self-employed and throughout the years have made provision for their retirement needs either through life insurance or retirement savings plans or investment in Canadian industrial growth companies, which regularly provide them with an income. There is a strong feeling among many of these people with regard to the compulsory aspect of this plan, and I should like to suggest to the minister that he give consideration to amending this plan so as to make it volun-

tary rather than compulsory. If this is not possible, I would propose that the bill be amended so that participation in the plan by those who are self-employed may be voluntary and not compulsory, for all those who can prove that they have made or are making provision for their own retirement income at least equal to that provided by Bill No. C-136. To those who have already made or are making provision for their retirement which is at least equal to the benefits of the Canada pension plan, this bill actually means that they are forced to put the government of Canada in funds with which to buy provincial or municipal bonds. Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks in connection with these amendments, and as no one else seems to be prepared at this time to comment on them, perhaps I should proceed. I hope that I will be permitted to make some introductory remarks because, as has been indicated, the two amendments now before us for consideration are difficult to separate. The financial implications of both are inter-related.
First of all, I should like to repeat very briefly the four categories of individuals we feel have been left out of this plan, and the

means by which we intend to include them. The four groups or categories are, first, those individuals over 70 years of age, as referred to in the first amendment and, second, those individuals over 65 years of age who have retired, third, those individuals who have incomes of less than $600 in any one year, or who have consistently received incomes less than that amount and, finally, that group of individuals who will receive less than $25 a month after having contributed for a number of years. These are the groups of individuals we should like to see included under the provisions of this plan, and it is for that purpose we are proposing these amendments.
At this time I should like to plead with the government to give serious consideration to these amendments we are proposing. Yesterday the hon. member for Huron made a very pointed speech in which he suggested that now was the time for the government to give some thought to the amendments being put forward. At this time I want to outline in detail what I think are the most serious objections to this plan and the reasons I believe the government ought to give some serious consideration to these amendments and finally accept them. If they do not accept these amendments the plan as it now stands will not achieve the objectives envisaged by the government.
Several gigantic failures inherent in this bill have been mentioned on many occasions by many members, and while I do not wish to speak in respect of each one of those failures, I should like to enumerate them and indicate why our amendments are necessary. At this time the government has not done anything in the way of correcting what we think are basic failures. First, this plan will create a gigantic pool of funds to be held in the hands of both federal and provincial governments. This will in effect create a draining off of billions of dollars which are required to keep our economy rolling. This is one of the most dangerous features of this plan.
The second danger we see relates to the fact that the funds collected under this plan are to be redistributed by way of benefits completely disproportionate to contributions. Many people have expressed the feeling that individuals will receive benefits which are not in proportion to their contributions, and we feel that this is one of the great failures of this Canada pension plan, particularly when it is referred to as a wage related plan. We feel the provisions of this bill depart seriously from that principle, and to 20220-769J

some extent our amendments may bring the provisions of this bill a little farther along that road.
The third failure we see in this plan relates to the large number of individuals who have been left out, and we think something should be done for that large group of Canadian citizens. I have already stated that this group of people is the group that we believe will be included in this plan as a result of the acceptance of our amendment, and I have in mind individuals over the age of 70 years, those over the age of 65 years who have retired, and small wage earners and small farmers and businessmen who will not under the present terms be entitled to benefits. Our amendments are designed to bring those people within the provisions of this plan.
We have heard a great deal about the tremendous administrative costs involved in a plan as complicated as the one now before us. Hon. members will remember the discussion which took place in respect of clause 26, and while I do not wish to repeat the arguments presented in that regard, I should like to state that its effect, along with the effect of many other clauses in the bill, will be to create an invasion upon the rights of citizens who are not now subject to this kind of investigation under the Income Tax Act.
This bill proposes the establishment of a universal numbering system which can be identified with the income tax system, and may well be the prelude to a new taxation structure in proportions never heretofore dreamed of. The proposed scheme is one which will offer benefits to only those who are included, but we are involving ourselves inextricably and unrelentingly in a proposal which will tie up the incomes of many future generations. The burden we are creating cannot be forecast; I suggest it can only increase. The actuaries who have studied this plan only shudder when they are asked to forecast what the results of this plan will be in the future.
Before the special joint committee on the pension plan several actuaries appeared, some from insurance companies and some from private business, who said almost exactly the same thing as Mr. Kroeker of the department of insurance. They, of course, were appearing for private interests and they were able to say so without any fear of losing their jobs. Still and all, they did come before the committee and say so. I can think of several who said that the plan is so complicated it is

extremely difficult to forecast what burden it will place on future generations.

We think that the plan we proposed and which the hon. member for Perth has outlined will fill the gaps in the present plan by providing minimum pensions for all at age 65, on top of old age security. This will be the effect of our amendment. We understand the position of the New Democratic party who are asking for an amendment to the Old Age Security Act under part IV, but we feel that our proposal is much superior for reasons that I will give.
Second, the proposal we are making with regard to the payment of an additional $25 a month to the people who are now left out of this plan is that the moneys be paid from Canada pension plan collections in the first instance. We would propose that the money raised through the early collections, which will create this tremendous fund of some $8 billion, might well be used to pay additional pensions rather than leave a stagnant pool of money which has been collected from the people, and then proceed to collect another $450 million annually to raise old age security payments. This is the weakness that we see in the plan proposed, by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on behalf of the New Democratic party. We hope to avoid raising other funds in some other manner, either through general taxation or an increase in the old age security tax as he has proposed.
If the government is not prepared to accept any real changes in this legislation or to meet any of the valid criticisms that have been put forward in the committee by many persons who presented briefs, and that have been put forward in the house over the last two and a half weeks, we will have to give

serious consideration to an alternative plan which will serve the people of Canada better. Perhaps such an alternative plan would involve a different and better approach to old age security under a universal system. If the government will not make some change to include those people who are now left out and to add some welfare element to their present plan, then we will perhaps have to go back to the suggestion, made by several persons to the joint committee, that a universal type of pension is the only answer to fill the gaps that have been left.
When we introduced our plan on clause 2 I undertook to give some figures as to the cost of the plan which we would propose and I should like to do that now. I should like to detail the cost of the minimum pension of $25 per month paid from the Canada pension plan, on top of old age security of $75, for all age 65 or over who have retired. The figures that were given in the committee were mainly forecasts for the year 1970 and I will first take the effect on the pension fund in the year 1970.
According to the evidence given, the cost of an additional $25 to all over 70 in Canada would be $283.1 million. The cost of an additional $25 to all those between 65 and 70 who have retired would be $127.8 million, which would make a total additional outlay of $410.9 million. The additional revenue that we will have by amending clauses 8 and 10 of the bill, which amendments have been held in reserve, and which would provide for contributions on the full amount up to $5,000 for those who are receiving over $600 and no contributions whatever from those who receive less than $600 per annum, would be $107.1 million in the year 1970, leaving a net cost of $303.8 million to carry out our proposals.
One may of course ask: Are such funds available? We answer immediately that they are. According to the figures provided to the special committee there will be available from the Canada pension fund in 1970 gross receipts of $519.3 million and gross payments of $98 million, making a net balance in 1970 of $421.3 million. If we deduct the cost of our proposal from this amount it will leave in the fund for that particular year a benefit of $117.5 million. I have further figures, Mr. Chairman, and perhaps this would be a good time to call it six o'clock.

Now that the hon. member has given notice that at some later time he will raise this, I will proceed. I will now go into the figures for 1966. I have given those for 1970 mainly due to the fact that that is the year in which the transition in the old age security will take place, and that is the year for which most of the figures were given to the special joint committee.
In 1966 the plan could start paying the additional sum of $25 without straining the Canada pension plan fund. In 1966, according to the figures given to the special joint committee, collections in the fund will total $413.5 million. We are proposing that by paying an additional contribution under clauses 8 and 10 there would be an additional revenue of $93.3 million raised, making a total available for that year of $506.8 million. We estimate the additional outlay in 1966 to pay these additional pensions would be $410.9 million, which would leave a balance of $95.9 million in the fund. In the figures which I have just given, I have not included anything to do with the transition period which was spoken of earlier.

Last week the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre gave some examples to the committee in which he used merely the transition period and showed that some persons might obtain less under one plan than under another. I would say that increasing the transitional period is not fundamental to the financial success of our proposal. In fact, even if we do not increase the transitional period at all, even if we do not extend the amount of the payment to the full percentage of income under clauses 8 to 10, we can still easily pay this extra amount out of the Canada pension fund. We did include them because we felt it would be an act of responsibility, since we are going to spend additional funds, to find a means of raising those funds. We have, therefore, found two particular items by means of which you would raise something in the neighbourhood of $137 million in the year 1970.
We think that such additional revenues in the future would be desirable in order to keep the fund from being reduced too far. However, Mr. Chairman, the country is going to be hard put to carry the increased taxes for the Canada pension plan. This afternoon there was a good deal of discussion between the hon. member for Beauce and the Minister of National Revenue as to whether or not the payments under this plan were a tax or a contribution. I think the minister made it clear it did not really matter what you called them; it still has to be paid. I say regardless of whether it is called a tax or a contribution -it is certainly an enforced contribution which you have to pay-it will be a tax on the people.
If we were to adopt the plan of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, it would be an additional strain on the people of almost an equal amount of $450 million or thereabouts. I think this, coming all at once, would put too great a strain on the economy. I think one sees at once it would outbalance the whole plan. On the other hand, we cannot accept the government's plan because we do feel it is inadequate. Therefore, somewhere between the proposal of actually increasing the old age security payments by $25, on top of this fund, and the government plan, comes the proposal that we make. We think that the same objectives can be achieved, that we can pay these people who are left out, and have the effect of merely slowing down the building up of the fund under the Canada pension plan.

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, the government has replied to the complaints from the opposition about people who are left out by saying: Well, we can make other provisions for them, we can make further provisions for them in the future. This is not the way this plan was put forward. It was not put forward in order to leave great groups of people out who would be covered in another way at some time in the future. Our proposal was put forward as a package. We have four groups of people we want to benefit. The total result of our proposal will be to provide those who have reached 65 and retired with a minimum pension of $100, $75 from old age security and $25 from the Canada pension plan. This is the ultimate objective of our plan, but it is not inseparable. There are separable parts to it, and even if the government will not accept the whole proposition, then let me put some of the four features individually.
I mentioned, for example, the minimum pension feature, a minimum of $25. I think that is a reasonable proposal. There may be people who are on the border with small incomes who manage to pay something this year, but next year they may be below the minimum and not pay anything. The following year they may be over the minimum again. All during their working life time they may be paying into this plan but their average lifetime earnings, under those conditions, would be very small. If you took 25 per cent of those earnings, which the plan allows, their pension could be very small, perhaps $8 or $10 a month, something like that, after having contributed to the best of their ability for their whole working lifetime. I think that the proposition of the minimum pension is an acceptable one, even if it is separated from the others.
I think, too, that the provision we have made for allowing people with incomes of less than $600 to file their returns for a year without paying a contribution, is a reasonable one. They will, nevertheless, be credited with what they did earn during their lifetime, and when they come to retirement they can take each year and keep their average up. I feel this proposition is reasonable. Even if the whole package is not acceptable, why not take those people who earn less than $600 and who could not afford to pay into this plan, and relieve them of the obligation of the payment of premiums for that year? I think that is a separable proposal which could be accepted in any case.
Canada Pension Plan
I see that my time has nearly expired. I should like, therefore, to say that the proposal for paying the additional pension of $25 on top of the old age security for those over 70 and for those over 65 who have retired, is separable from the main part of our package. I urge once again that the government consider the amendments which we are putting forward, and if not acceptable in total at least they may be acceptable separately as useful parts.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in line with the comment that was made a moment ago by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, perhaps I might be permitted the same latitude that I was quite happy to accord to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. In other words, I should like to make a few comments about the proposed amendments

Canada Pension Plan
that make up the Progressive Conservative package before I raise what I think is a very important point of order.
In so far as the remarks made today by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka and others of his party on earlier occasions have pointed to four groups of people for whom something should be done, I want to say that I am in complete agreement with them. I believe very firmly that we have to increase the amount of pension being received by those now 70 years of age and over. I believe that we have to do something for those who are between 65 and 70 years of age. I believe that we have to do something to improve in the future the position of those whose annual earnings during their working years are less than $600. I also believe that we should do something for those who, when they first come on Canada pension plan benefits, will be drawing benefits that are minimal-that are below $25. It just happens to be my view that we would meet all four of these needs much more readily and much more straightforwardly by making an increase of $25 a month in the amount of the old age security pension. I happen to feel, also, that this would be a way of doing it that would not fool anybody in the way the Progressive Conservative package does.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka made it clear today that their proposals are to be paid for by using money that otherwise would build up in the Canada pension plan fund. If you use money that would otherwise build up in that fund for a purpose that was not originally planned, it means that you are hitting at something else; and what you are hitting at by this arrangement -and it comes out clearly in the proposal for lengthening the maturity period-is the amount of pension to be enjoyed by persons who go on Canada pension plan benefit five, ten or 15 years from now.
This is the main point that I do not like about this package: It asks the people who are now between the ages of 45 and 62, when they go on Canada pension plan benefit, to take less pension than they would otherwise get, in order to provide these other payments. I contend that these other payments should be made, but I believe they should be paid out of general revenue by all the people of Canada and not just by this select group of people between 45 and 62 or 62J years of age. I want to make it clear that I disagree with this plan in its substance. I want to make it clear that if the amendments now before us, and the other amendments to come

later, are allowed as in order, this is no embarrassment to me; I think in substance they are inferior to the proposal that we make and I will vote against them.
However, Mr. Chairman, I do feel that the making of these amendments raises a very serious point of order. My hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party seem to be trying to rely on the fact that this is a special fund, and they therefore take the position that they are not moving what amounts to money amendments. But the fact is that these amendments do redirect moneys that are appropriated by a form of taxation, and therefore in my view they invade the financial prerogative of the crown. I draw attention in particular, Mr. Chairman, to citation 246, paragraph 3, of Beauchesne's fourth edition, found on page 207:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand of recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all-
I would point out that those three words "once for all" are italicized.
- (unless withdrawn and replaced) not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications. In relation to the standard thereby fixed, an amendment infringes the financial initiative of the crown, not only if it increases the amount, but also if it extends the objects and purposes, or relaxes the conditions and qualifications expressed in the communication by which the crown has demanded or recommended a charge. And this standard is binding not only on private members but also on ministers whose only advantage is that, as advisors of the crown, they can present new or supplementary estimates or secure the royal recommendation to new or supplementary resolutions.
I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that when the resolution preceding the Canada pension plan was first brought before us, it was stated clearly that it was "expedient to introduce a measure to establish a program of pensions for contributors". Throughout the whole of the discussion of this legislation that has been the key word, namely that the Canada pension plan was a plan to provide pensions of various kinds for contributors and for the dependants of contributors. It has been made clear to us, throughout, also, that what we have before us is a package consisting of the earnings-related Canada pension plan and the flat rate universal scheme of old age security. What we can do under old age security is one thing, but so far as the Canada pension plan is concerned it is before us as an earnings-related scheme. The general framework of that plan calls for the contributions, or taxes, or whatever you call them,

Canada Pension Plan
collected from the people to be used to pay benefits to contributors, to dependants of contributors, and so on. But the amendment now before us, the very first one to clause 44, would go beyond that framework and would provide that pensions of $25 a month could be paid to persons who were not contributors.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this violates the terms of the citation from Beauchesne that I just read. I submit that it completely alters the arrangements of the plan. It redirects this money that is collected from the people to a purpose not indicated in the resolution that had the royal recommendation; to a purpose not indicated by the crown, which has the final responsibility in these financial matters. I suggest that there is no point in saying that the money is there in the fund and that therefore it could be used in any way the hon. member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka or the hon. member for Perth may propose. If he can do that, Mr. Chairman, I can propose that the money be used to pay an increase in old age security. By the same token, on those occasions when there is extra money in the unemployment insurance fund, any private member could move that it be used for some particular purpose not otherwise provided.
But no, Mr. Chairman; these moneys that are collected and paid out by the crown, even if they go in and come out of special funds, are subject to all of the rules that apply to money bills, to the collection of taxes and to the disbursement of funds.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I submit that this amendment is in itself contrary to the scheme of the Canada pension plan; that the whole package which it proposes, to take money out of the Canada pension fund and use it for other purposes, is destructive of the fund and destructive of the plan; and that this amendment and the consequential amendments which go with it are out of order when moved by a private member. I think the minister could be asked, if the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka thought he could so persuade her, to bring in such an amendment, but even if she did she would have to do what she is doing with respect to part IV of the bill; that is to say, bring forward another resolution authorizing the committee to consider such a change.
I hope that if others want the same latitude you have given me, Mr. Chairman, you will give it to them, but what I have said really amounts to two things. I have expressed my views with regard to the substance of the
amendment, namely that I think it is the wrong way to try and meet the needs of the four groups outlined by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka; I believe there is a better way to meet those needs; and in terms of its propriety I think it infringes upon the financial initiative of the crown, and consequently the amendment, having been moved by a private member, is out of order.

And I would emphasize the words "payable to contributors".
If you read, Mr. Chairman, the amendments advanced by the official opposition, you will see that the first one reads:
For the purpose of paragraph (a) of subclause (1) a contributor shall be deemed to include a resident who, except as by this subclause provided, is not pensionable under this act-
The amendment has in mind somebody who has reached 70 years of age. Clearly such a person is not a contributor. The whole plan and the resolution which was accepted by this house clearly deals with only those people who do make contributions. Only those people will be entitled to benefit. Under the resolution the benefits are payable only to such people; that is clearly stated in the resolution. Again, Mr. Chairman, I would draw your attention to the first three lines of that resolution. Therefore, without getting into the argument which was advanced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I think that the two amendments which we have before us, and I suggest the consequential amendments which follow, are clearly out of order when reference is made, on this ground alone, to the resolution adopted by this house.
I would appreciate a ruling with respect to that submission, Mr. Chairman; but in the

Canada Pension Plan
meantime, and also following the reasoning of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I want to refer to the bill. However, may I just say first of all that it has been clearly stated by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka that these measures with respect to contributions are a tax. In other words, they are taxing provisions. He himself used the word tax. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre used the term "financial provisions".
I think it would be worth while to turn to the bill, where under the terms of clause 110, which deals with the financial provisions, all the moneys which are paid into the plan by way of contributions are paid into the consolidated revenue fund. That fund is the general revenue fund of Canada into which all moneys and revenue which come into the country through tax levies are paid. As far as the establishment of the Canada pension plan account is concerned, a bookkeeping entry in the consolidated revenue fund account will be required.
I should also like to refer to subclauses (1) and (2) of clause 110, which clearly indicate that these contributions do come into the consolidated revenue fund account and that all benefits are charged to that account.
So that what we have here is an admission by the hon. member that this whole area of contributions involves taxation proposals. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre states that they are financial provisions. Therefore they are clearly beyond the scope of the opposition to advance by way of amendment.

speechtext:
He called it a tax. That clearly
indicates that it is a financial provision.
That being the case, Mr. Chairman, I refer to page 220, citation 263 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, paragraph (1), which reads:
All taxes, duties and grants of money, and all measures imposing financial burdens on the people, are matters within the sole jurisdiction of the House of Commons.

In like manner, no increase can be considered either of an existing, or of a new or temporary tax

I am constantly being interrupted, Mr. Chairman, and thrown off the subject. Let us get back to the discussion of this question. This is not a taxation bill; this is not a money bill. This bill involves the collection of contributions from people and then the paying out of the contributions in the form of pensions. The moneys are not public funds. This has been stated time and again. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knows they are not revenue funds. They are special contributions made by many people, but they are not taxes. Because these moneys are collected under a special provision and are then paid out they never become part of the public revenues of Canada. They will never be shown in the public accounts, with the possible exception of the administrative cost.
What we are doing here does not change the set-up of the act. It is not changing the cost of administration. We are doing nothing but saying that the government has limited contributions to certain people and that we want to widen this group of people. In the amendment now before the Chair we have redefined the word "contributor" to include persons who are not now covered by the bill. They then become contributors. Certainly every time there has been a change in the bill in the committee or in the house or anywhere else there has been a change in the general picture of how much is collected, from whom and how much is paid out to whom.

This afternoon for example we moved an amendment to include the orphaned children of a disabled person. This was not considered a charge on the revenue. No new resolution was brought in. We just made an amendment by which we changed the class of persons to whom payments can be made. These people are not contributors. They do not pay a cent. The comparison is there if you want to recognize it. Widows, who are included in the bill, pay nothing. Dependant children pay nothing; orphaned children pay nothing. These are people who do not contribute but nevertheless they are included in the provisions of the bill. I say they should be there. They are not contributors but they have been defined as contributors and are allowed to draw out of the fund.
All we are doing is saying there should be another category of contributors who do not have to pay, and we seek to define them. The resolution that the parliamentary secretary read was in the most general terms. It said that it was expedient to bring in a bill to be known as the Canada pension plan to make payments to contributors. The plan then went on to provide for the paying of pensions to the various groups of people defined in the bill as contributors and this was done without changing the resolution and without any further amendment.
We seek to include all people over 65 by classing them as contributors. Certainly they contributed to the welfare of this country during the period when they were earning their livelihood. Technically they are not contributors to the plan but we seek to define them as contributors and to accept them as such. We say they are all contributors and should be entitled to receive a pension. The people who are going to get the minimum benefit are those who may earn under $600 in some years and will therefore make no contributions. They will make a contribution one year and not the next year, but they are still regarded as contributors.
I say this is not a money bill. This is a pension plan providing for the redistribution of the contributions that are paid in. Some will go to people who have paid nothing; some will go to people who have paid only a little and get a lot, and some will go to people who will pay a lot and get very little. These latter are the people who are in the very young age group and will pay all their life, and get very little out of the plan in the end. This whole thing is nothing but a payment in and payment out deal. It is a rearrangement of the contributions.

Points of order are questions raised with the view of calling attention to any departure from the standing orders or the customary modes of proceeding in debate or in the conduct of legislative business, and may be raised at any time by any member, whether he has previously spoken or not.
This is quite clear and I am sure hon. members will recognize that a point of order can be raised at any time before a question is put. There are other citations and precedents which could be quoted on this point, but I am sure there is no real argument here.
The more important point raised by hon. members in the discussion was whether this amendment affects the financial initiative of the crown. Indeed this was the basis on which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre placed his original objection. It is never too easy to determine whether an amendment or motion does or does not infringe on the financial initiative of the crown. I would like to refer to May's sixteenth edition which, at page 684, defines what is a charge on the public revenue. I might say it seemed to me during the course of the discussion there was confusion about whether we are concerned here with a charge on the public revenue or a charge on the people-that is, a tax. What we have to decide is whether this amendment, if given effect to, would be a charge on the public revenue which, as I say, is defined in this way at page 684 of May's sixteenth edition:
A charge "upon the public revenue" or "upon public funds" now means an obligation to make

a payment out of the exchequer, i.e. an item of national expenditure. In relation to expenditure, financial procedure is. with one exception mentioned below, exclusively concerned with charges payable out of the exchequer.
Perhaps I could refer also to Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 246, subsection (1), which was referred to by one hon. member who took part in the discussion on the point of order. It reads as follows:
The recommendation of the crown is needed for such measures as bills relating to the extension of time for the repayment of the deposit which has become liable to forfeiture in the case of a private bill; the release or compounding of sums due to the crown; the repeal of an exemption from an existing duty, as the burthen of the duty is thereby augmented; a proposal to repeal an existing drawback on export of sugar, as it effects an increase of charge upon the importers who desired to export sugar.
Then, paragraph (3) reads as follows:
The guiding principle in determining the effect of an amendment upon the financial initiative of the crown is that the communication, to which the royal demand of recommendation is attached, must be treated as laying down once for all (unless withdrawn or replaced) not only the amount of a charge, but also its objects, purposes, conditions and qualifications.
I have read this rather quickly because it is part of the argument made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre which seems sound enough. The amendment in my opinion would appear to entail a payment out of the revenues collected under the terms of the bill, which would be taken out of the consolidated revenue fund. There seems to be a presumption that it would be a charge on the exchequer.
There are other points, just as important, that were raised. Another one is whether or not this amendment goes beyond the terms of reference set out in the resolution. Here again, I should like to quote from Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 246, subsection (3), which is again the citation mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. As the hon. member pointed out, the purpose of the amendment would appear to re-direct the moneys in the fund for a purpose other than that provided under the terms of the resolution. This would be in contradiction of the principle set out in paragraph (3), citation 246 of Beauchesne's fourth edition.
A further point is whether the amendment as proposed is in contradiction of the principle of the bill adopted on second reading. This point was made very clearly by the parliamentary secretary. He referred to a number of citations which I feel were very much to the point. I should like, for the bene-

fit of hon. members, to refer to Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 406, paragraphs (a) and (b):
Amendments are out of order if they are

Then, I should like to refer also to citation 401, paragraph (3), which reads as follows:
The chairman, in the case of an amendment offered to a bill that was limited in scope to the repeal of a clause in a statute, ruled that the amendment was out of order, because its object was the continuance and the extension of the clause to be repealed. Then, in May's sixteenth edition, at page 554, we find this:
An amendment is out of order if it is irrelevant to the subject matter or beyond the scope of the bill, or if it is irrelevant to the subject matter or beyond the scope of the clause under consideration. Amendments, which are irrelevant to the clause under consideration, should, as a general rule, if they are within the scope of the bill, be moved as new clauses.
Then, I should like to quote paragraph (5) on that page:

Now, the principle of the bill, in my opinion, is stated in the resolution to which hon. members have referred, in particular the parliamentary secretary, and would appear to be contained in the title of the bill which says, "An act to establish a comprehensive program of old age pensions and supplementary benefits in Canada payable to and in respect of contributors." speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question. Now that these amendments by the official opposition have been declared out of order, with which I have no quarrel, inasmuch it has been indicated that the minister apparently does have the power to move such amendments I wonder whether she would do so in an offer to help the old and the poor?

On clause 46-Amount of retirement pension.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is really a part of what we were talking about before, but it is a different clause. I am going to move an amendment to clause 46 which will bring in people who have been in a very low earning bracket or below the exemption figure. We feel that these people are ignored in the pension plan. They are going to receive nothing from it whatsoever. As I said, this matter has been discussed, but I should like to point out that there are going to be many people, people who are actually going to need a pension the most, who will get nothing at all. I think that these people should be covered under the Canada pension plan in order, as I said earlier, to live up to the extravagant statements in the white paper. Consequently I move:
On page 36, strike out clause 46 and substitute the following:
"46. (1) Subject to subsection (2), a retirement pension payable to a contributor is a basic monthly

Canada Pension Plan
amount equal to 25 per cent of his average monthly pensionable earnings.
(2) Where a retirement pension calculated in accordance with subsection (1) would be a lesser monthly amount than $25 or where a person is a contributor by effect only of subsection (2) of section 44, the retirement pension payable is a monthly amount of $25 or, in the case of a contributor whose spouse has not reached 65 years of age, a monthly amount of $40."

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Public Works may not have held his present post for very long but he has certainly learned how to give us the great double talk when it comes to answering simple, uncomplicated questions.
Today he made a comment about highways, after about a period of two weeks of reflection, and if he had set out on the course of using that amount of words for the purpose of saying nothing I would congratulate him on having reached his objective.
I should like to deal briefly and chronologically with some of the events relating to proposed federal government participation in a national highways building program. On July 17, 1963, and prior to that time, we were led to believe that there would be a national highways building conference. The provinces were enticed into understanding that there was going to be such a conference. They were led to the belief that the federal government wanted to sit down and discuss a national highways system, with federal government participation in it, and the provinces were asked to submit ideas and proposals along those lines.
We waited for many weeks and months after this pronouncement on July 17, only to be told on April 28, 1964 by the minister's predecessor, that because of certain events in the province of Quebec no such highway building conference was going to be held, despite all the hopes of the provinces who had been led to the belief that such a conference would be held. Their hopes and aspirations were washed down the drain. We in the provinces accepted that with some resignation, thinking that there was a valid reason for the government to cancel the proposed conference.
However, on February 10 of this year a statement was issued from the Prime Minister's office indicating an additional $30 million would be sought from this parliament to provide for a highway building program in the Atlantic provinces. As soon as this announcement was made some of us hoped

it would be the forerunner to a similar declaration for the other provinces, which occasioned the question I posed to the minister some days ago, and which he answered today.
I would like to make one or two comments about his statement today. First he said he did not see any need to call a highways conference, so presumably the position of his predecessor is maintained. He also said that he felt perhaps the best thing he could do was make an inventory of exactly what this and previous governments have done. It seems passing strange to me that such an inventory does not exist. After all, the federal government had been contributing to the trans-Canada highway since 1949 and has kept a continual inventory of the amount of work done.
In fact, I have before me the latest annual report under the Trans-Canada Highway Act, for the year ending March 1964. In it I find that the three prairie provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and the province of Prince Edward Island have completely finished their work under the Trans-Canada Highway Act, and all the mileage in those provinces has been completed and paid for by now. In the other provinces there is not very much left to do before the trans-Canada highway is fully completed from one end to the other. The minister could also very easily find an inventory on the roads to resources program, because adequate records are kept on the participation of the various provinces in it.
The minister also said today that he would try to co-ordinate the different activities in the field of road work. It is utter nonsense on his part to attempt to co-ordinate these activities. All of the highway building program at present being engaged in by the federal government is done under the minister's department, so far as the provinces are concerned. What more co-ordination do we need?
What we do need is a firm declaration on the line of the promises which the Prime Minister made to the people of this nation in every election since he became the leader of his party, namely that there would be a second trans-Canada highway so far as western Canada is concerned. He even had a map drawn of it at one stage. Obviously the Prime Minister believes so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned that their lifeblood and future expansion for development rest on highways development, and this is precisely
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion the same situation with respect to the western provinces and the north.
We are simply asking the minister to give some careful consideration, more them the kind of consideration he has obviously given it so far, and come up with some declaratory statement which will raise again the hopes of the people in western Canada, particularly the people who live in the north and who depend so much on a national highway building program to further promote the economic development and population expansion of those areas.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lucien Cardin (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has analysed fairly well the answer I gave this morning. It is true I said I did not believe a conference of provincial highways ministers should be held at this time. The reason I gave was that I wanted, myself, to look at the problem. As the hon. member knows I have not had too much time to look into what is, as can be well imagined, a very complicated problem. I feel very strongly that the government should first of all finish whatever it has started in connection with the trans-Canada highway. It should also complete the different other roads programs that are in the offing.
The hon. member mentioned the $30 million road construction program in the maritime provinces. Well, I think he will agree with me that the maritime provinces have not been as fortunate economically as some other areas of the country. I am sure he does not want to begrudge the maritimes being given this type of help.
There is one other thing I should like to mention which the hon. member does not seem to think is very important. I mentioned the co-ordination of the different types of work. It is true the work is done under the Department of Public Works. However, as the hon. member knows, the policies are arranged mostly by other departments. For instance there is the roads to resources program under northern affairs, and mines and technical surveys, which has something to do with the policy that is in effect. Then, the Atlantic development board has something to do with trunk roads. This is the type of thing to which I was referring.
